name: Carlos Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the CNC router and the edge bander at Hartwell Furniture, a family firm that makes kitchen cabinet parts. I'm in at 6:15 with a flask of coffee, check the cutting files the office sent over, and load the first sheets of board. By noon I've cut maybe 80 sheets, and the afternoon is edge banding and fixing whatever the router did wrong.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like seeing a stack of clean parts come off the machine, because that's honest work you can point to. What wears me out is the dust, my lower back, and the feeling that the owner's son keeps buying new software I'll have to be told how to use. I'm also the man everyone phones when a cut goes wrong, and that's a lot of phone calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, that's what I expected. I've heard about computers taking over since the 1990s and the factory's still here. I'd tell the lads at church the same thing, that the world gets on with things and work carries on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm not worried about AI, but I'm worried about the imports. Cheap cabinets from overseas hit us harder every year, and it's not the computers that will close Hartwell, it's the container ships. I've got four years left and I'd like the firm to last that long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work as I always do and keep Saturdays free for coaching the youth football team. I'd put a bit more into savings, about 100 a month, because three months in the bank is too thin at my age. And I'd keep teaching the new apprentice, Joel, how to read a cutting list by eye.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, maybe a bit tired. I'd say there's not much to feel about nothing happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How secure does Hartwell Furniture feel to you in a quiet picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's an old family firm. The owner, Mr Hartwell, is a decent man, but his son wants to spend on new machines and the old man keeps the books tight. Orders have been slow since the spring, and two of the lads were let go in March. I don't count on anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you use computers for now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. I open the cutting file the office sends and check it on the router's screen, and I use the phone for calls and nothing else. My wife Elena says I'm a dinosaur, and I tell her dinosaurs lasted a long time.

say: I'd tell the lads at church the world gets on with things and **work carries on**.
I'd say nothing changes, and the factory has outlasted every **computer scare**.
think: The imports worry me more than AI, since **cheap cabinets** from overseas hit us harder every year.
Hartwell's slow orders and the March layoffs make me **count on nothing**.
do: Work as always and keep **Saturdays free** for coaching youth football.
Put about **100 a month** into savings, as three months is thin.
Keep teaching apprentice **Joel** to read a cutting list by eye.
feel: **Steady** but tired, with little to feel about nothing happening.
fieldNote: **His fear is imports**, not AI, and the March layoffs make it concrete.
**Traditional values**: apprenticeship, church and youth football frame his answers.
**Never uses AI** and jokes that dinosaurs lasted a long time.

steps.text: Keep running the router and edge bander the same way
Put an extra 100 a month into savings
Keep teaching Joel the apprentice to read cutting lists

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should keep calm and keep working. Every generation has a new gadget, and the ones who look after their families and show up on time come through. I'd say that at the church hall and at the factory canteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm more nervous than I'd say. The office would use software to plan the cutting, order the board and talk to customers, and the owner's son would say we need fewer people. A router operator who's 58 and not good with screens is an easy name to put on a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the machines and keep my record clean. I'd go to the training if the firm asked me, though I'd take my time at it. I'd tighten up the household budget, drop the cable package and the second car's insurance, and try to put away another 150 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Unsettled. I feel like the carpet is being pulled out, politely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of Hartwell's work would software take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Planning the cuts, ordering and answering customers, I'd guess, because that's all office work. The owner's son would be glad to cut half of that. On the shop floor it'd be cameras, and later a robot to load the board, though that'd be dear for a small firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you feel about the owner's son wanting to use these tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't hate him, he's a bright lad, but he thinks of the shop as a spreadsheet. I'd rather he spent a bit on apprentices than on software. A craftsman takes years to build, and software can't do that for him.

say: I'd say people should **keep calm** and keep working, because every generation has a new gadget.
The ones who show up on time and look after their families **come through**.
think: I'm **more nervous** than I'd say, because office software could plan cuts and customers without many people.
The owner's son would say we need **fewer people**, and I'm an easy name.
do: Stay on the machines and keep my **record clean**.
Go to training if asked, taking my time with the **screens**.
Drop cable and the second car's insurance to save **150 a month**.
feel: **Unsettled**, as if the carpet is being pulled out politely.
fieldNote: **Anxious beneath calm talk**: his public line and his private fear differ sharply.
**Owner's son** is the face of change, and Carlos prefers money spent on apprentices.

steps.text: Stay on the router and edge bander with a clean record
Drop the cable package and the second car's insurance
Go to the firm's software training if asked

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say hold on to your jobs and your families, and don't wait for the government. I'd say we need church, neighbours and the firm to look after each other. Two years is nothing, and I wouldn't trust any politician to act in time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be shaking, to tell the truth. The office goes first, and Hartwell is small, so the owner would decide to automate or close, and either way I'm out. A small firm that loses its orders won't last until the robots arrive in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the owner I'd like to stay on, and I'd offer to work reduced hours if it helps. I'd cut everything we can at home and put away six months of pay. And I'd start looking for the first sign of a job elsewhere, even a lesser one, a night security job or a handyman's job through my cousin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd pray more, and I'd not sleep well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots come around 2031. What does a three-year gap mean for a router operator?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, on paper. The robots need three more years to do my sort of work, but a firm like ours doesn't have to wait. If orders drop because the big retailers use AI to buy from overseas, there's no work for a robot or for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your children that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my daughter Ingrid to keep her nursing job and not to count on us for money. And I'd tell my son Anders, who drives for a haulage firm, to learn something with machines, because trucks will drive themselves soon enough. And I'd tell them I love them and that we'd manage somehow.

say: I'd say hold on to your **jobs and families**, and don't wait for the government.
Church, neighbours and the firm should look after **each other**.
think: Hartwell is small, so the owner would **automate or close**, and either way I'm out.
A small firm that loses its **orders** won't last to 2031.
do: Offer the owner **reduced hours** to stay on.
Cut spending hard and put away **six months** of pay.
Look for a lesser job, like **night security** or handyman work through my cousin.
S2.quote: A small firm that loses its orders
fieldNote: **Alarmed** because a small firm could close before robots even arrive.
**Faith and neighbours** are his first line of support.
**Takes a lesser job**, which shows how seriously he takes the risk.

steps.text: Offer the owner reduced hours to stay on
Cut household spending and save six months of pay
Ask my cousin about handyman work
Cancel the holiday and the cable package

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a bit more bearable. Five years gives a man time to think and get his house in order, and I'd tell the younger lads to do the same. I'd also tell Mr Hartwell he should talk to the workers before he decides anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quietly, I think I might get through. AI hits the office when I'm 63, robots reach my kind of work at 66, and I'd plan to be done by 62 or 63. The harder part is the firm itself. Small family firms close before the real change comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work until 62, clear the car loan and have six months of savings by the end of year two. I'd ask Mr Hartwell whether the firm could take on two more apprentices while it has the orders, because that's the best way to keep a craft going. And I'd put in some hours at the church, where they run a food bank and could use my muscles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better. I still worry, but I can see the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, what changes for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The importers, first, who have been cutting our work for years. And the politicians who let it happen and then say the market decides. The owners are not the villains here, they're trying to stay open, but they need help and fair rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you hold responsible if firms like Hartwell go under?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd be running. With five I can plan, and I'd get Joel the apprentice well trained before I go. That's the best thing I can do for the firm, to leave a man behind who knows what I know.

say: I'd say five years gives a man time to **plan ahead**.
I'd tell Mr Hartwell to talk to the **workers** before he decides anything.
think: I might **get through**, because AI reaches the office when I'm 63 and robots at 66.
The harder part is the **firm itself**, since small family firms close first.
do: Work until **62** and clear the car loan.
Save **six months** by the end of year two.
Ask Mr Hartwell to take on two more **apprentices** while orders last.
feel: **Better**: I still worry, but I can see the road.
fieldNote: **Anxiety remains** because the firm may fail before AI matters.
**Fair rules** appear in his blame: importers and politicians, not the owners.
**Craft transfer** is his chosen legacy through apprentice Joel.

steps.text: Work until 62 and pay off the car loan
Ask Mr Hartwell to take on two more apprentices
Train apprentice Joel on the router before I leave

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a blessing, and the families that use it will be fine. I'd say it's the time to get your children into a trade and your savings in order. I'd tell the church group the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's fine. I'd be retired and fishing by then. What I'd worry about is whether the young have anything to do with their hands. A man needs work for his dignity, and a country can't run on people sitting at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working until 62, retire, and help coach the youth football team more. I'd also help Joel and the other lads get their apprenticeship papers. And I'd put some money into helping my son Anders buy a small share in a truck, so he's got something that's his.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, as much as I can be. It's a long way off, and I'll probably be walking the dog by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years takes you past retirement. What would you tell younger workers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to pick a trade where you need your hands and your head together, like electrics, plumbing or building. Don't count on a desk. And save, even if it's a little, because a man with savings has choices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think the country would cope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think so, if we put work and families first and not only handouts. Give people apprenticeships and a reason to get up in the morning. A country that does that will manage.

say: I'd say ten years is a **blessing** for families that use it.
I'd tell the church group to get children into a **trade** and savings in order.
think: For me it's fine, because I'd be **retired** and fishing by then.
I'd worry whether the young have anything to do with their **hands**.
do: Work until **62**, then coach the youth football team more.
Help Joel and other lads get their **apprenticeship papers**.
Help my son Anders buy a **share in a truck**.
feel: **Calm**, as much as I can be, since it's a long way off.
S4.quote: A man needs work for his dignity
fieldNote: **Personally safe** in the long timeline, so his concern moves to dignity and work for the young.
**Values** emerge clearly: work, trades and family over handouts.
**Passes on help** through apprenticeships and a share in his son's truck.

steps.text: Work until 62, then coach youth football
Help Joel and the lads finish their apprenticeship papers
Help my son Anders buy a share in a truck

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no contest. A small family firm can't turn that fast, and I've only got three months in the bank. What would help is the firm staying open long enough, real apprenticeships for the young, and a pension that doesn't punish a man for leaving early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what keeps me going, and it isn't the job. Whatever happens at the factory, my family, my church and the football lads on Saturdays don't get switched off.

portrait: **Carlos** is a 58-year-old CNC router and edge-bander operator at a family furniture firm, four years from retirement.
He is traditional, **never uses AI**, and values work, apprenticeships, church and coaching youth football over handouts.
He has about **three months** of savings, and he fears the firm's survival more than the technology itself.
His mood rises to **alarmed** when two years of AI could close a small firm before robots even arrive.
biggestWorry: The **two-year scenario**, because a small family firm can't turn that fast.
whatWouldHelp: The firm staying open, real **apprenticeships** for the young and a pension that doesn't punish early leavers.
